newsitem.title: USA: Clinton Medicare plan gets tough Senate reception.
newsitem.headline: Clinton Medicare plan gets tough Senate reception.

text.p: President Clinton's recently unveiled Medicare plan was billed as an effort to meet Republicans halfway on the sensitive issue, but some lawmakers made it clear Thursday the White House still has miles to go. Republicans, and some Democrats, warned the White House at a Senate Budget Committee hearing that they had serious concerns with the plan Clinton announced earlier this week to reduce Medicare spending by $138 billion over six years.

Lawmakers from both parties cautioned that the White House proposal to cut spending on health maintenance organizations by $46 billion over six years went too far and could make it tough to expand managed care to more of the 38 million senior citizens who rely on Medicare.
"This will discriminate against the good guys and (those plans) who are efficient. I will oppose it strongly," said Oregon Democratic Sen. Ron Wyden.

Republicans said the plan did not address Medicare's long-term financing problems. They were scathing in their criticism of a Clinton proposal to transfer part of Medicare's fast-growing home health program from the Part A hospital trust fund, which faces bankruptcy, to another Medicare fund.

Republicans estimated the White House plan would move upwards of $100 billion in 10-year home health costs out of Part A, which is funded by payroll taxes. They called it a "gimmick" and "shell game" that made the Part A trust fund, now expected to go bankrupt in 2001, appear more robust.
Texas Republican Sen. Phil Gramm termed the transfer "completely beyond the range of possibility" predicting there was "not a chance in the world" it would pass a key panel.
Office of Management and Budget deputy director Jacob Lew, testifying before the committee, did not provide figures for the size of the transfer but said it was under $100 billion.

Lew said that by using the home health transfer, the White House was able to ensure the solvency of the Medicare Part A trust fund through the start of 2007 -- fulfilling a promise to protect the program for a decade.
"This policy avoids the need for excessive reductions in payments to hospitals, physicians and other health care providers," Lew said.
He also defended the White House plan to cut payments to HMOs, saying data showed Medicare was paying them too much and losing money on every senior citizen who chose managed care.

"This reflects a reasonable step in terms of the magnitude of savings we could get from HMOs," Lew said. Other witnesses said HMO cost controls were possible, but the White House plan for across-the-board cuts was not the right way.

Not all the reviews were bad. Republicans applauded the White House decision to recommend roughly $22 billion in savings above Clinton's last Medicare proposal. They were pleased with initiatives to impose cost controls on skilled nursing care and, separate from the contentious transfer, an $18 billion reduction in home health payments.
House Republican leaders in a news conference later Thursday took a more upbeat tack, saying they hoped to wrap up Medicare prior to other parts of any budget deal.
Senate Republicans were still licking their wounds from the November elections when Democrats attacked them for a failed proposal to reduce Medicare by $270 billion.
"The administration proposal is a test of Christian values on this side of the aisle," said New Hampshire's Judd Gregg.
The Clinton plan carefully avoids big increases in premiums, instead cutting providers. Clinton said Wednesday he might support forcing well-off seniors to pay more.
